Ryan has it right. The MLR point estimates are the same as ML.

If you want bootstrapped CIs with MLR:

Step 1. Estimate with MLR to get scaled fit (and check for surprises with a quicker run). Disregard tests of parameter estimates.

Step 2. Estimate with ML and bootstrap to evaluate parameter estimates with respect to their CIs. Disregard fit.

Pat

messages.body_plain:
I am not 100% certain how the value of "estimator" translates to other options. If I read the document correctly, then setting the "estimator" to "MLR" will set "estimator" to "ML", "test" to "yuan.bentler.mplus", and "se" to "robust.cluster."

Therefore, one possible way to do that in one single call to sem is setting the arguments as below:

estimator = "ML", test = "yuan.bentler.mplus", se = "bootstrap"

This is an illustration:

```
# Example adapted from https://lavaan.ugent.be/tutorial/mediation.html

options(width = 132)
library(lavaan)
set.seed(1234)
X <- rnorm(100)
M <- 0.5*X + rnorm(100)
Y <- 0.7*M + rnorm(100)
Data <- data.frame(X = X, Y = Y, M = M)
model <- ' # mediator
             M ~ a*X
             Y ~ b*M
           # indirect effect (a*b)
             ab := a*b
         '
fit_mlr <- sem(model, Data, estimator = "MLR")
set.seed(4143)
fit_boot <- sem(model, Data, estimator = "ML", se = "bootstrap")
set.seed(4143)
fit_boot_mlr <- sem(model, Data, estimator = "ML", test = "yuan.bentler.mplus", se = "bootstrap")
summary(fit_mlr)
summary(fit_boot)
summary(fit_boot_mlr)

# The following two sets of SEs should be identical (bootstrapping SEs)
parameterEstimates(fit_boot, boot.ci.type = "perc")$se
parameterEstimates(fit_boot_mlr, boot.ci.type = "perc")$se

# The following output should have SEs different from those above (ML SE)
parameterEstimates(fit_mlr)$se

# The following two outputs should have the same p-values (scaled)
anova(fit_mlr)
anova(fit_boot_mlr)

# The following output should have a different p-value (unscaled)
anova(fit_boot)
```

I tested this only for a single-level single-group model. Not sure if this also works for more complicated models.

-- Shu Fai

messages.subject_clean: A quick reference for the available estimators
messages.body_plain:
I know there is a pattern in the naming of the estimators (MLM, MLMV, MLMVS, etc.) and the help page also describes the meanings of all the possible options. However, I would like to have a quick reference table so see what each shorthand does. I could not find one and so I prepared one myself.

To my understanding, if no missing data in the dataset, lavaan will translate the value of the estimator to options for estimator, se, information, and test. I wrote a script to list the settings for each estimator:

```
mod <-
"
m ~ x
y ~ m
"
dat <- as.data.frame(MASS::mvrnorm(100, c(x = 0, m = 0, y = 0), diag(3)))
# Only documented
estimators <- c(
"ML",
"MLR",
"MLM",
"MLMV",
"MLMVS",
"GLS",
"WLS",
"WLSM",
"WLSMV",
"ULS",
"ULSM",
"ULSMV",
"DLS",
"DWLS",
"MLF"
)
fits <- sapply(estimators,
               function(x) sem(mod, dat, estimator = x),
               simplify = FALSE,
               USE.NAMES = TRUE)
fit_options <- lapply(fits, function(x) x@Options)
options0 <- c(
"estimator",
"se",
"missing",
"information",
"test"
)
fit_options0 <- t(sapply(fit_options, function(x) unlist(x[options0]),
                       USE.NAMES = TRUE))
fit_options0 <- as.data.frame(fit_options0)
fit_options0 <- fit_options0[order(fit_options0$estimator,
                                   fit_options0$se,
                                   fit_options0$test), ]
print(fit_options0, quote = FALSE)
```

This is the table (may not display correct in email browser):

```

DLS         DLS         robust.sem listwise     expected     expected    satorra.bentler
WLSM       DWLS         robust.sem listwise     expected     expected    satorra.bentler
WLSMV      DWLS         robust.sem listwise     expected     expected     scaled.shifted
DWLS       DWLS           standard listwise     expected     expected           standard
GLS         GLS           standard listwise     expected     expected           standard

MLMVS        ML         robust.sem listwise     expected     expected  mean.var.adjusted
MLM          ML         robust.sem listwise     expected     expected    satorra.bentler

ML           ML           standard listwise     expected     expected           standard

ULSM        ULS         robust.sem listwise     expected     expected    satorra.bentler
ULSMV       ULS         robust.sem listwise     expected     expected     scaled.shifted
ULS         ULS           standard listwise     expected     expected           standard
WLS         WLS           standard listwise     expected     expected           standard
```

Are there any options that I overlooked and should be included?

-- Shu Fai

messages.subject_clean: Benefits and drawbacks of treating x (covariates) as fixed vs. random?
messages.body_plain:
If I have a simple regression or mediation model with observed variables, the default setting in lavaan (at least the sem() function) is to fix the exogenous observed variables to the sample statistics.

If I turn fixed.x = FALSE or mention the exogenous variables in the syntax, they become treated as 'random', I suppose, and the means/variances etc. are estimated along with the rest of the model.

I am guessing the main argument against treating the exogenous covariates as random is that the normality assumption then applies to them, as well? Are there any other common arguments for or against treating those variables as random?

I am coming from the perspective of a survey researcher where the exogenous variables are rarely actually fixed in the sense of a randomized experiment. Is it 'cheating' to treat x as fixed even if they are just observations along with the rest of the columns in the dataset?

messages.subject_clean: Combine FIML and ML to improve estimation time?
messages.body_plain:
Rogier--
     No specific insight, but this reminds me of ML vs GLS from the dawn of factor-based SEM. Joreskog figured that GLS, which inverts the empirical covariance matrix rather than the model-implied covariance matrix, would be faster than ML because the empirical matrix does not change, so the matrix inversion needed to be done only once, instead of with every iteration. But he found that ML converged in fewer iterations. Between more, faster iterations vs fewer slower iterations, it was a wash.
     I do wonder why FIML with complete data is so slow. That may be a code issue which could be improved. How old is the code?
--Ed Rigdon

An interesting topic.

I checked and I believe the bottleneck is in finding the data patterns. You can try this:

library(profvis)
p_c_fiml <- profvis(sem(myModel, data=mydata_complete,missing='fiml'))
p_c_fiml

Only very limited information is available in the plot if you do not load the source of lavaan. Nevertheless, you can still see that a lot of time is spent identifying the missing data patterns by lav_data_missing_patterns().

One reason for Hybrid FIML to be faster, I believe, is because the task to identify missing data patterns is partially done before calling lavaan::sem(), by separating the dataset into two parts, one with complete data and one with missing data. lavaan::sem() does not need to spend time to identify the missing data patterns for half of the data.

> I am guessing the main argument against treating the exogenous covariates as random is that the normality assumption then applies to them, as well?

Correct, but in practice, it doesn't really matter when the exogenous variables are complete (i.e., the estimates are not biased).

> Are there any other common arguments for or against treating those variables as random?

If you have incomplete exogenous variables and want to use FIML, you would have to either set fixed.x=FALSE or set missing = "fiml.x".

There is also the additional setting conditional.x=TRUE (available when fixed.x=TRUE). messages.body_plain:
> The first factor has 2 items and the second factor has 3 items. The factors are orthogonal to each other.

Then how is your model identified?  With only 2 indicators (and the factor is not substantially correlated with another factor), identification requires fixing both loadings to 1 (to estimate the factor variance), or at least to equality (if factor variance is fixed to 1).  You cannot test invariance in this case because in the configural model, all loadings are already equal (if fixed to 1), or at least statistically equivalent to being equal (i.e., you would not gain any df if you constrained loadings across groups because you would have to also free factor variances across groups).

I suspect the model is not identified, even if lavaan was unable to find evidence enough to issue such a warning.

http://ww.w.statpower.net/Steiger%20Biblio/Steiger02.PDF

Terrence D. Jorgensen
Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

> instead of an additional 15 df (15 constraint loadings), I only get +10

Right, because you need to free the 5 factor variances in Group 2.  When loadings are constrained to equality, fixing factor variances to 1 in *both* groups is not necessary for identification.  If you left them fixed, you would be testing equivalence of loadings *and* variances.  When std.lv <http://std.lv>=FALSE, the variances are free in both groups already, and you only constrain 10 loadings because 5 reference indicators have loadings fixed to 1.  But those are statistically equivalent parameterizations for continuous data (you can even mix/match when comparing configural to metric invariance).

However, you are requesting DWLS, which is designed specifically for categorical data (i.e., the weight matrix contains sampling variances of threshold and polychoric-correlation estimates).  Yet you aren't declaring any variables as categorical---perhaps they are already of class c("ordered","factor") in the data.frame dat?

If they are ordinal, then you cannot meaningfully compare factor loadings across groups unless thresholds are constrained across groups.  Constraining thresholds links the response scales across groups, so you can actually test whether a 1-unit increase in the factor corresponds to the same expected increase (in the same units) of the latent response underlying the categorical indicator.

If you set parameterization = "theta", they should have the same absolute value, but opposite signs.

The latent response scale is unknown by definition, and so must be arbitrarily identified.

https://www.statmodel.com/download/webnotes/CatMGLong.pdf

https://doi.org/10.1080/10705510701758406

In the GLM framework, the location and scale of the latent response are typically identified by fixing the threshold to zero (to estimate an intercept) and fixing the residual variance to 1 ("conditional" or "theta" parameterization).  In the SEM framework, the default in Mplus and lavaan is to fix the intercept to zero and estimate the threshold, and to fix the total variance to 1 ("marginal" or "delta" parameterization).  This is arbitrary; either way, the threshold is a certain distance above/below the arbitrary mean of the latent distribution, with units arbitrarily determined by which variance you fix.  Alternatively, you could fix 2 thresholds (in polytomous data) and estimate both the mean/intercept and (residual or marginal) variance given the fixed distance between the 2 fixed thresholds (this approach is used by LISREL).

W =~ ... + ... + ...
M=~  ... + ... + ...
W.M =~ ... + ... + ...

Jurgen--
     Broadly, taking "statistically significance" to mark estimates as qualitatively different from each other is not consistent with guidance from the American Statistical Association (Wasserstein, Schirm & Lazar 2019):
https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.1080/00031305.2019.1583913?needA
. P-values change, but estimates don't go to zero. If you are not centering your main effects before creating interactions, you might try that, as it will make parameter estimates easier to interpret in light of the likely collinearity between main effects and interaction terms.
     But to answer your question, this is not uncommon. If the interaction model is correct, then the model with main effects only is misspecified, and the predictors included in that model are correlated with the excluded interaction term. This appears to be happening in your results.

messages.body_plain:
> 1) What formula does lavaan currently use to compute SRMR and RMSEA for ordinal models when using ULSMV estimation?

The lavaan developer is the third author on that paper :-)  Use the lavResiduals() function, which uses the right formulas.

But lavaan has not incorporated that ad-hoc formula for correcting the RMSEA (or CFI/TLI) when chi-squared is mean- AND variance-adjusted (only for mean-adjusted stats).  The reason is that even the author who proposed it (Savalei, 2018 <https://doi.org/10.1080/00273171.2018.1455142>) cautioned that it is only appropriate for MLMV (continuous nonnormal data), not ULSMV or (D)WLSMV for categorical data.  Nonetheless, that is the method Shi et al. (2020) employed.

Savalei (2021 <https://doi.org/10.1080/00273171.2020.1717922>) more recently proposed new solutions that perform better, which I expect will eventually be incorporated into lavaan.

> 2) The R code provided in the supplementary materials notes that the function works for ordinal factor models and listwise deletion should be used when you have missing data. Is it correct then to assume that this has not been extended to structural models and lavaan.mi objects?

Correct.  For lavaan.mi objects, I apply the same formulas lavaan does to calculate chi-squared-based fit measures, but using the pool chi-squared.  I have not adapted lavResiduals() to work with lavaan.mi objects, and that to-do list is a long way out.

Hi Sophia,

A couple of notes:

1) I have to run my model (let's say one similar to the example one below) for 300 different outcome variables (e.g. 300 different Y's). Is there any way to correct my MC confidence intervals for multiple comparisons? Sort of, if you change the level of the CI (e.g. from a 95% CI to a 99% CI) that will change the alpha level you use. A X% CI is equivalent to (1-alpha)*100 so a 95% CI corresponds to an alpha of .05 and a 99% CI corresponds to an alpha of .01. If you wanted you could use a Bonferroni correction to adjust the level of CI for multiple corrections. As far as I know, more complex adjustments for multiple comparisons (e.g. a Holm correction) wouldn't be possible without a bunch of programing on your side.

2) According to the output that I get with this method, ALL of my indirect effects are significant  (i.e. the point estimate lies within the interval) across my 300 runs of the model for separate outcome variables. My model is more complex than a simple mediation, and for any indirect effect that look at within the model, the MC comes out as significant. This seems highly unlikely. Does anyone know what might be going on? What do you mean by the "point estimate lies within the interval" if you're talking about the point estimate for the parameter of interest (e.g the indirect effect), this should always happen since a CI is an interval estimate of a parameter and the point estimate should be within the interval. For hypothesis testing with CIs you'd see if a value based on the null hypothesis (often a value of 0) lies within the CI.

Also note that I have about 20.000 observations. That's a lot of power, it's entirely possible all indirect effects are significant.

One other note: I'd recommend using the newest version of semTools and the MonteCarloCI function instead of MonteCarloMed, the function has been updated, provides CIs for multiple parameters at once, and provides a smoother interface with lavaan.

Alex

> Pseudo-R^2 of McFadden, Loglikelihood-indices and LR-Test?

These are all calculated from log-likelihoods, which are only available using ML estimation.  lavaan does report R^2 on the latent-response metric, which is McKelvey & Zavoina's pseudo-R-squared.

https://stats.idre.ucla.edu/other/mult-pkg/faq/general/faq-what-are-pseudo-r-squareds

You can still use the lavTestLRT() function to conduct a (scaled/shifted) chi-squared-difference test, which is a LRT when the models'  chi-squared values are each a LRT.

An alternative is pairwise ML (estimator = "PML"), but that would not enable calculating the (full-)likelihood-based pseudo-R-squareds because it is a product of all uni- and bivariate likelihoods.  But the lavTestLRT() function nonetheless provides corrected information criteria.

https://users.ugent.be/~yrosseel/lavaan/pml/PL_Tutorial.pdf

messages.body_plain:
Ah, that's a really good question. I've been meaning to work on a paper related to three-way interactions among latent variables. Here's what I'd say (note: this is my opinion I don't have a simulation study demonstrating this (yet)):

If you have the same number of indicators for all first order latent variabels (X, Z, & W) and the indicators are congeneric (have similar factor loadings) I'd use a matched-pairs approach. This will greatly simplify your model compared to the all pairs approach

If you're using the all pairs approach with residual centering you should allow covariances of all product indicators based on the same item for latent interaction variables at the same level. So you'd estimate a residual covariance between X1.Z1 and X1.Z2 and X1.W1. For these you could then constrain them to be equal (to reduce the number of parameters to estimate)if they have the same first order indicator. For the three way interaction you would allow residual covariances between product indicators based on the same variable, e.g. X1.Z1.W1. and X1.Z1.W2, you'd constrain parameters to equality if they had the same pairs of indicators, e.g. X1.Z1.W1 and X1.Z1.W2 would be equal to X1.Z1.W1 and X1.Z1.W3. Note you do not have to include residual covariances between product terms for the 2-way and 3-way interactions since the residual centering process means that the 2-way interaction variables are uncorrelated with the 3-way interaction variables.

Hope that helps

Alex

messages.body_plain:
> I used the semTools::measurementInvariance() function

Don't.  It is based on outdated ideas that do not pan out in practice (e.g., testing scalar invariance when metric is already rejected; using change in a fit index as a complementary test or effect size).  There is a reason the function is deprecated.

> do I interpret these results as if there is metric invariance (because cfi.scaled is acceptable) or not (because the change in chi square is significant (there are coupe of thousands of participants) and delta cfi is 0.029)?

I would definitely reject the null hypothesis of metric invariance.  With your large N, chi-squared certainly has a lot of power to detect small differences in measurement properties, but the most liberal criterion I have ever seen for change in CFI was < 0.01 (which is as terrible an idea as any other such criterion; this is not what CFI was designed to tell you).

With only 3 indicators, I think your only recourse is to fit 3 competing partial-metric-invariance models (each one freeing a different indicator's loading, while the other 2 are equated).  If any of them are statistically indistinguishable from configural-invariance fit (i.e., fail to reject H0), then you found your baseline to test partial scalar invariance.  But you might not find any pair of indicators whose loadings can be validly constrained to equality across groups, in which case the latent scales cannot be reliability linked across groups, preventing any meaningful comparison.

Assistant Professor, Methods and Statistics
Research Institute for Child Development and Education, the University of Amsterdam

Satorra, A., & Bentler, P. M. (2001). A scaled difference chi-square test statistic for moment structure analysis. Psychometrika, 66(4), 507–514. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02296192

You don't say what book you mean by "in the book," but that is the most common way to code a nominal predictor in regression, yes. The coefficient for Forage.1 in the first equation, for example, would be the model-implied difference in NH4.N between "cm" and "bm" (the 0/0 group, or reference group) holding Period.daily.Rainfall and Air.Temp constant.

Assuming you're working in significance-testing framework, I also generally recommend testing with a multiple-df test (either Wald or likelihood ratio) constraining the coefficients of Forage.1 and Forage.2 to zero simultaneously, as that is the test of "no effect of forage type."

All that said, since you're operating in an SEM package, you have the option of treating the three levels of forage as a grouping variable and running a multiple-group model, which would give you more flexibility. There are examples in the lavaan tutorials for the syntax, and in any SEM reference (e.g., Kline's textbook free online) for the logic.

Pat

Hi everyone,

I am seeking to correct my Monte Carlo-derived CI's for indirect paths in lavaan for multiple comparisons.
I am attempting to stay away from applying a Bonferroni-centered solution. This would imply changing my alpha level and thus the level of my CI, but given that I have to correct for over a hundred tests this becomes too stringent. Therefore I am seeking to apply an FDR-analogue solution.

A proposed solution for a similar problem  (link to source <https://stats.stackexchange.com/questions/147917/false-coverage-rate-for-confidence-intervals-of-positive-likelihood-ratios-of-mu>) is to control the CI's for the false coverage rate. But this solution requires me to undergo parameter selection first, by for instance, thresholding the p-values associated with said parameters.

The problem is, as far as I understand,  I cannot take this 1st step of selecting a number of parameters for whom to compute the CI's as the p-values associated with indirect effects in lavaan are non-informative (due to the sampling distribution associated with indirect parameters being non-normal). Which is why I use the Monte Carlo method to get my CI's in the first place.

I wonder, the following:
If the False Coverage Rate solution is actually valid in this context
 If there is an alternative to using p-values for selecting the parameters that I will then compute FCR-corrected CI's for. I thought of making my selection equal to my number of parameters, but mathematically this seems to lead to the same alpha level. See equation in Algorithm 2.1 in source [1].
If there is any other method out there for dealing with this issue.

References to the False Coverage Rate solution can be found here:
[1] Rosenblatt, J. D., & Benjamini, Y. (2014). Selective correlations; not voodoo. NeuroImage, 103, 401–410. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuroimage.2014.08.023
[2] Benjamini, Y., & Yekutieli, D. (2005). False Discovery Rate–Adjusted Multiple Confidence Intervals for Selected Parameters. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 100(469), 71–81. https://doi.org/10.1198/016214504000001907

Thank you.

Sofia

> multi-group or multi-level models and I've had a few goes but I'm not sure entirely either are possible with the combinations of latent measures, mediation, ordered factors and bootstrapping?

Multilevel is not available in lavaan for ordinal outcomes.  Even if it were, level-2 N=7 is a really bad idea.  Better to regress all observed variables on 6 dummy codes to control for their (average) effects.

But multigroup is an option, if you have a substantial N (e.g., 500+ for stable DWLS results) in each group, and that would give you an idea about between-country variability.  But between-country comparisons will only be possible if (at least partial) measurement invariance of mat_mh holds across countries.  Bootstrapping works fine with multigroup models, too.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Terrence,

Thank you for your answer!  My sample size is ~20.000.

Just to clarify:
1) Do you mean that, given that my sample is large enough, I do not have to worry about my underlying ab distribution for an indirect effect being non-normal? (As it approximates a normal distribution)
2) If yes to the above: I could then use the p-values that lavaan gives me for the indirect effects? (and just FDR correct them afterwards).

Concerning your second suggestion:
Thank you for clarifying that I don't have to base my selection on p-values.
If I were to rank my candidate parameters by the absolute value of their unstandardized estimates it is not clear to me what is a cut-off that I can then use to select a given (high-ranking) subset of them, to then compute CI's for with the method in the link. My question is, what should I use as a cut-off here?

Thank you!

Best, Sofia

> How large is your sample?  For all the fuss people make, the delta method actually works quite well asymptotically.  I hope N is quite large given how large your model is, and if so, I would recommend passing the relevant subset of parameterEstimates() output to p.adjust() to request the FDR correction.
>
> Alternatively, you could use the method described in the CrossValidated link.  You don't need to base your decision on p values.  If the H_0 = 0 for all candidate parameters, you could rank them in order of absolute value of their (un)standardized estimates.

messages.body_plain:
Sofia,

Jumping in for Terrence:

On the first section, yes and yes. With N=20,000, in most research contexts, anything that is practically significant will be statistically significant. And with that power, the decrement from using the a*b p-value instead of an asymmetric CI will be so small as to be meaningless. So you can do the easy thing and be fine.

Pat
